extracted.intended_audience: readers of Laurence Sterne / general literary readers and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and embedded evaluative remarks within a literary narrative about how to read, name characters, and reason — chiefly applicable to readers and students of fiction. Contains authorial asides that function as prescriptive comments on reading habits and naming choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active, reflective reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind should be accustomed to make wise reflections, and draw curious conclusions as it goes along; do not read straight forwards merely in quest of the adventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator reproves the habit of reading straight for plot alone and imposes a 'penance' to re-read a chapter to catch inferences; cites Pliny the younger's maxim that even a bad book yields profit when read reflectively. Example/anti-pattern: readers who skip subtle hints and sly communications lose the moral and erudition a book can impart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful selection of character names (names influence character)
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a strange kind of magick bias, which good or bad names... irresistibly impressed upon our characters and conduct; therefore names matter and can shape a person's destiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The father's systematic opinion: some names are 'neutral' (Jack, Dick, Tom), some positive (William), some negative (Tristram, Nick/is the DEVIL). He even wrote a dissertation on the name 'Tristram' and warns that the injury of a bad name 'could never be undone.' Use names deliberately; avoid careless or injudicious naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature judgments from scant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not take it absolutely for granted from an unguarded word or two (e.g., that the narrator is a married man); strict justice requires more evidence before forming a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator admonishes a reader who jumps to the conclusion that he is married from a few phrases and instructs them to withhold judgment until better evidence is produced. Practical advice for readers: seek fuller textual proof before drawing biographical or interpretive conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of ideas that begin as whim but settle into dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: Notions that enter the brain as mere whims and 'a vive la Bagatelle' may after free entrance claim settlement there, working like yeast or starting in jest and ending in earnest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator warns learned readers against indiscreet reception of such guests (fanciful opinions); implication for critical practice: interrogate the origin and staying-power of eccentric hypotheses and test whether they are playful fancies or defensible positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective persuasion blends rhetoric and practical instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquence: persuasion hung upon the father's lips; the elements of Logick and Rhetorick were so blended up in him — he persuades despite not having read classical rhetorical authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the father's skillful orations and disputations (ad hominem turns, shifting voices and characters). Guidance for writers: rhetorical force can come from practical acumen and knowing your respondent's weaknesses as much as from formal training; adapt argumentative tone (christian, heathen, husband, father, patriot) to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer trusted experienced practitioners to 'next best' substitutes (applies metaphorically)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we cannot get the very thing we wish, never to take up with the next best in degree to it; that's pitiful beyond description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: mother's choice of an old midwife over a scientifically trained male operator. As a general principle (read as advice to makers/readers): value genuine expertise and be cautious of settling for inferior substitutes when stakes are high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to subtle moral and scholarly hints, not just carnal action
rubrics_metrics.description: The subtle hints and sly communications of science fly off... the heavy moral escapes downwards; both are as much lost to the world as if left in the bottom of the ink-horn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of readers' 'vile pruriency' for fresh adventures — instructs readers (and by extension writers) to craft and look for subtle, moral, and erudite layers that require attentive reading to appreciate.
